Employee Onboarding Workflow

Purpose
This workflow standardizes how new employees are prepared, welcomed, and enabled to become productive in their first 30 days. Because the company operates across customer support, merchandising, logistics, and technology teams, onboarding must align people, equipment, system access, compliance tasks, and manager expectations. This workflow applies to all regular employees and should be adapted for interns and contractors where required.

Pre-Start Preparation
Once a signed offer is received, HR creates the employee profile in the HRIS within one business day and opens an onboarding checklist. The hiring manager confirms the job title, reporting line, start date, work location, schedule, and department cost center. IT receives a provisioning request for email, collaboration tools, device setup, and role-based application access. Payroll is notified of compensation details and employment classification. If the hire is remote, Facilities or Workplace Operations coordinates shipping of equipment and any welcome materials.

Required Documentation
Before day one, the employee must complete identity verification, tax forms, direct deposit setup, confidentiality agreements, and policy acknowledgments. HR reviews the packet for completeness at least one business day before the start date. Missing items are escalated to the hiring manager and the new employee with a clear completion deadline. No employee may begin handling customer or payment-related information until required employment documents are complete.

Day One Agenda
The manager owns the first-day experience. At minimum, the schedule includes a welcome meeting, team introduction, review of role expectations, explanation of training milestones, and a walkthrough of communication channels. HR delivers a company overview session covering values, code of conduct, attendance expectations, security basics, and support resources. IT verifies account access, multi-factor authentication enrollment, and device readiness. The employee should leave day one knowing where to find policies, who approves requests, and what success looks like for the first month.

Week One Enablement
During the first week, the employee completes functional training assigned by the department. Customer-facing staff review service standards, escalation rules, and case documentation requirements. Operations staff review order lifecycle, shipping exceptions, and approval thresholds. Corporate staff review applicable internal controls, collaboration practices, and reporting routines. Managers must schedule at least two check-ins during week one to answer questions and confirm that systems, tools, and schedules are functioning correctly.

Thirty-Day Milestones
By day 30, every new hire should have completed mandatory compliance training, met key collaborators, reviewed team metrics, and handled a limited but meaningful portion of their role independently. Managers should document progress against a simple ramp plan that includes training completion, work quality observations, and any support needs. If onboarding gaps emerge, the manager creates a corrective enablement plan with specific due dates and owners.

Ownership and Escalation
HR owns the master onboarding checklist, the hiring manager owns role readiness, and IT owns technical access delivery. Delays longer than one business day for critical access or required documents must be escalated to People Operations and the department leader. Managers should not assign production work that exceeds the employee's completed training level.

Quality Control
HR audits a sample of onboarding files monthly to confirm documentation, completion dates, and policy acknowledgments. Findings are shared with department leaders to improve readiness, reduce avoidable delays, and ensure that onboarding remains consistent across locations and functions.
